540.title: Mothers of the believers
540.hook: the Prophet's wives are called mothers of the believers (33:6)

540.howItsDone: Muslims call the Prophet's wives the mothers of the believers, say 'may God be pleased with her' after their names, and learn their lives from the sira and hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: uswah, the beautiful example, found in a trench. Your line was do the hard thing with them.

Khadijah. 'A'isha. Hafsah. Umm Salamah. Names you'll hear in Muslim families, called across playgrounds and written on school forms. In Muslim books, each is usually followed by a short phrase of honor: may God be pleased with her. Behind each name is a woman with her own story. And the Qur'an itself gives them, together, a title that turns a household into a family for a whole community. It's in Surah Al-Ahzab.

Pickthall: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their selves, and his wives are (as) their mothers." Ummahat al-mu'minin: the mothers of the believers. The title meant honor and respect. It also meant, as the surah says later, that no one could marry them after the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Who were they? The biographies list the women married to him at different times. Khadijah first, a widow and a merchant, remembered by tradition as the first to believe in his message; a report in Sahih Muslim says he married no one else while she lived. Sawdah, a widow who had emigrated to Abyssinia. 'A'isha, daughter of Abu Bakr, a great teacher of the early community; a large share of the hadith come through her. Hafsah, daughter of 'Umar, with whom the first gathered written pages of the Qur'an were kept. Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, called the mother of the poor for her charity. Umm Salamah, whose advice at Hudaybiyyah helped calm a crisis. Zaynab bint Jahsh, known for working with her hands and giving the money away. Juwayriyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Maymunah. Many were widows. Several came from families or tribes that had been at war with the Muslims. Biographers describe some marriages as alliances, some as acts of protection, and some as matches of affection. Sunni and Shia Muslims both use the title, and both honor Khadijah deeply; they differ in how they view some of the wives' roles in the conflicts after the Prophet's death. What the verse gives is a family: every believer, it says, has these mothers.

541.title: Men and women, side by side
541.hook: a verse naming believing men and women equally, ten qualities each, with one reward (33:35)
541.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 33:35 when teaching that men and women share the same spiritual duties and the same reward, and many learn its ten pairs of qualities by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khadijah, first of the mothers of the believers. Your line was some were widows, some were matches of affection.
screen: `SOME WERE WIDOWS, SOME WERE MATCHES OF AFFECTION.`

segments.voice: A woman in Medina has been listening to the Qur'an for years. It's beautiful. It speaks to everyone. But she has noticed something, and she says it out loud: why does it seem to address the men, and not mention us? According to a report in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, it was Umm Salamah, one of the mothers of the believers, who asked. Other reports, one of them in Tirmidhi, name other women. And the answer, the reports say, came as a verse.

Pickthall begins it: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe". And it keeps going, pair after pair, ten times. The devout men and women. The truthful, the patient, the humble. The men and women who give in charity, who fast, who guard their chastity, who remember God much. Then one ending for all of them: God has prepared for them forgiveness and a vast reward. In Arabic it sounds like a drumbeat: al-muslimina wal-muslimat, al-mu'minina wal-mu'minat. The masculine plural, then the feminine, again and again. Arabic grammar normally lets the masculine plural cover everyone. This verse refuses the shortcut and names the women every single time. Notice what the ten qualities are. Not roles, not jobs: surrender, faith, devotion, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity, fasting, chastity, remembrance. The inner life, and the practices that shape it, each open to both and named for both. And the reward isn't split. One forgiveness, one vast reward. Muslims discuss many questions about men's and women's roles, and scholars and communities answer them differently. This verse is one that people on many sides of those conversations quote, because on the things it lists, its answer is plain. Both, equally.
screen: `MEN WHO SURRENDER, AND WOMEN.` · `TEN QUALITIES, TEN PAIRS.` · `THE GRAMMAR REFUSES THE SHORTCUT.` · `ONE FORGIVENESS, ONE REWARD.`

segments.voice: Go through the ten slowly: surrender, faith, devotion, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity, fasting, chastity, remembrance. Which one do you see in someone of the other sex in your life, a sister, a brother, a colleague, a parent, a friend, and notice it's one you're trying to grow too. If you pray, you can pray for that person by name.

542.title: Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ
542.hook: Allah and His angels send blessings on the Prophet, so do the same (33:56)
542.howItsDone: Muslims say or write sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam after the Prophet's name, recite the Abrahamic blessing near the end of every prayer, and many count salawat on Fridays or on prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umm Salamah, and a verse that names women and men, pair after pair. Your line was both, equally.

Look at any page of a Muslim book, a sermon transcript, a social media post about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. After his name, there's a small curl of Arabic calligraphy, or four letters in brackets, or the words peace be upon him. It can start to feel like punctuation. But it isn't a habit someone invented to be polite. It comes from one verse in Al-Ahzab, a verse that says who does it first, before anyone on earth.
screen: `ONE VERSE SAYS WHO DOES IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Verse fifty-six. Pickthall: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." Look at the order. First Allah. Then the angels. Only then the believers, asked to join something already happening. The Arabic word is salat, the same word as the daily prayer. Bukhari records an early explanation from Abu al-'Aliya: Allah's salat is His praise of the Prophet before the angels, and the angels' salat is their prayer for him. When believers send it, it's a request: O Allah, bless him. Blessings like these are called salawat, and a common form begins Allahumma salli, O Allah, send blessings. The small curl in print stands for sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam: may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Many Muslims say it aloud or write it when his name comes up. Many count them, too, because a hadith in Sahih Muslim says that whoever sends one blessing on the Prophet, Allah sends ten blessings on that person. One out, ten back. Near the end of the daily prayer, Muslims recite a longer salawat, often called the Abrahamic blessing, asking that Muhammad and his family be blessed as Ibrahim and his family were blessed. Sunni and Shia Muslims both include the Prophet's family in it; the exact wording varies by school. So the little curl is the end of a long chain: Allah, the angels, and then anyone who reads the name and stops for one breath.
screen: `ALLAH, THEN THE ANGELS, THEN THE BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, or want to try, say the short form ten times, quietly, counting on your fingers: Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammad, O Allah, send blessings on Muhammad. If that isn't your practice, sit with the verse's picture instead: a blessing already moving, from Allah, through the angels, and an invitation to join in. Either way, end in silence.
Salawat. Blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, what Allah and the angels send first, and what believers ask for, one blessing out and ten returned. Today's word.
Your line: blessings on him. One verse, and a long chain behind the little curl. That's the last of Al-Ahzab.

543.title: The mountains sang with Dawud
543.hook: the mountains and birds echo Dawud's praise, and iron is made soft in his hand (34:10–11)
543.howItsDone: Muslims honor Dawud as a prophet given the Zabur; beautiful Qur'an recitation is still praised by comparing it to his voice, and many Muslims glorify Allah aloud or quietly with subhanallah throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salawat, blessings that start with Allah and the angels, then reach the believers. Your line was blessings on him.

Stand in a stone stairwell, or under a highway bridge, and hum one low note. The walls hum it back. Children find this out on their own, and then they do it twice. Surah thirty-four, Saba', opens its stories with a man whose praise did that on a scale no stairwell could manage. He sang, and the hills answered. The birds joined in. And the same hands that held the song could bend iron like clay. His name is Dawud, the David of the Psalms.

Verse ten. Allah gave Dawud a grace, and then speaks to the landscape. Pickthall: "O ye hills and birds, echo his psalms of praise!" The verb, awwibi, carries the sense of returning, again and again, the way an echo does. The hills don't just hear him; they give the praise back. Surah Sad says it too: the mountains glorified with him at nightfall and at sunrise, and the birds gathered. In the Qur'an, Dawud is given the Zabur, a scripture Muslims connect with the Psalms. A hadith shows how his voice was remembered. When the Prophet ﷺ heard his companion Abu Musa reciting beautifully, he told him he'd been given one of the flutes of the family of Dawud. A voice like Dawud's became a way to praise a reciter. Then verse ten turns: and We made the iron supple for him. Verse eleven tells him to make coats of mail and to measure the links well. The singer is also a smith. Another hadith adds that Dawud ate only from the work of his own hands, though he was a king. The same man lifts praise so beautiful the mountains join, and sits at a workbench getting the rings of armor the right size. The verse ends with an instruction to him and his family: work righteousness. Worship and work, in one pair of hands.
screen: `A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAWUD.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, or want to try, quietly hum or say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, a few times, letting the sound fill your chest. If that isn't yours, hum one low note and feel where it lands, in your body, then in the room, as the room gives a little of it back. Then let the sound stop, and sit in the quiet it leaves.
Awwibi, the word telling the hills to echo Dawud's praise, again and again, like a returning echo, while the birds join in. Today's word.

544.title: The staff and the termite
544.hook: Sulayman dies leaning on his staff, and only a termite eating it reveals his death to the jinn (34:14)
544.howItsDone: Muslims believe knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb) belongs to Allah alone, and many scholars cite this verse when warning against fortune-telling and claims that jinn reveal hidden things.

segments.voice: Yesterday: awwibi, the hills echoing Dawud's praise. Your line was the mountains sang along. Today, his son.

A king stands leaning on his staff, watching his workers. They are jinn, beings of smokeless fire, building for him: high halls, statues, basins like wells. They work hard, because he's watching. Time passes. He doesn't move. They keep working. Then something tiny, something none of them noticed, finishes its own quiet job inside the wood. The staff gives way. The king falls. He had been dead the whole time. This is Sulayman, son of Dawud, and one of the Qur'an's quietest death scenes.
screen: `HE HAD BEEN DEAD THE WHOLE TIME.`

segments.voice: Surah Saba', verse fourteen. Pickthall: "nothing showed his death to them save a creeping creature of the earth which gnawed away his staff." The Arabic is dabbat al-ard, a creature of the earth. The verse doesn't name the species. Commentators understand a woodworm or termite, which is where today's title comes from. How long Sulayman stood there, the Qur'an doesn't say. Some commentators guess a long while; the text is silent. Then the point: when he fell, the jinn saw clearly that if they had known the unseen, they wouldn't have kept on in humiliating toil. Here's why that stings. Commentators explain that jinn were thought to know hidden things, and fortune-tellers claimed their help. And here are the jinn, working at full speed for a master who can't see them, fooled by a man leaning on a stick. The only one who knew was a small creature chewing wood. In the Qur'an, the unseen, al-ghayb, belongs to Allah. Not to jinn, not to kings, not to anyone with a reputation for secret knowledge. And a second, gentler point. Sulayman, who had armies and wind and jinn at his command, died as everyone dies, here standing up, in the middle of an ordinary day. The verse doesn't mock him. It just tells the truth about how little anyone knows.
screen: `A CREATURE OF THE EARTH, EATING THE STAFF.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you'll see today, and quietly list what you don't actually know about them: what they're carrying, what they're afraid of, what happened this morning. Let the list get long, and notice how much of a day runs on guesses. If you'd like, rest in the verse's idea: what's unseen is held by Someone, not by anyone's guesses.
Sulayman, son of Dawud, the king whose staff was gnawed through by a small creature while the jinn kept working, unaware he had died. Today's word.

545.title: The broken dam
545.hook: the people of Sheba are given two gardens, turn away, and the dam bursts (34:15–17)
545.howItsDone: Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after, and scholars often cite the story of Sheba when teaching that gratitude (shukr) preserves blessings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sulayman, whose death only a small creature knew. Your line was only the termite knew.

Nobody thanks a light switch. A gift that works every day goes invisible. Surah thirty-four carries the name of a people, Saba', Sheba, whose gift was water, held back and shared out across their fields. Near Ma'rib in Yemen, old stone ruins of a dam still stand, and commentators connect them with this story. The surah tells it in three short verses, and it isn't really about engineering at all.

Verse fifteen. There was a sign for Sheba in their homeland: two gardens, one on the right and one on the left. The instruction that came with them is short. Pickthall: "Eat of the provision of your Lord and render thanks to Him. A fair land and an indulgent Lord!" That last line is almost a postcard: a good land, and a Lord who forgives. Verse sixteen: but they turned away. So Allah sent on them sayl al-'arim, the flood of the dam, or as some translate it, the overwhelming flood. Their two gardens were exchanged for gardens of bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote trees. Verse seventeen gives the reason in one word: kafaru, they were ungrateful. Classical dictionaries connect the root, k-f-r, with covering over. Ingratitude covers a gift, like soil over a seed, until you stop seeing it. The Qur'an doesn't list a dramatic crime. Nobody told them to do anything hard. Eat, and give thanks: that was the whole instruction, and it was the thanks they let go. Commentators connect the burst dam with the dam at Ma'rib; the Qur'an itself doesn't give a date or name the dam. It names the pattern: a gift received without gratitude starts to come apart, and what replaces it is thin and bitter. A few verses earlier, about Dawud's family, the same surah says it plainly: few of Allah's servants are thankful.

If you can, pour a glass of water and hold it, and think about where it came from: rain, a river, a reservoir, a pipe someone laid. Take a slow sip. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, the praise belongs to God, as many Muslims do after drinking; if not, simply notice the gift in your hand.
Sheba, the people with two gardens and every provision, whose own ingratitude brought the flood that broke their dam. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude keeps the garden. Two gardens, and one small instruction. Day five hundred forty-five, done.

546.title: Wings in twos and threes
546.hook: He made the angels messengers with wings, two, three and four (35:1)
546.carry: he adds to creation as he wills
546.howItsDone: Belief in angels is one of the six articles of faith in Islam; Muslims understand them as unseen beings made of light who carry out Allah's commands, known only through the Qur'an and hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sheba, two gardens lost when the thanks ran dry. Your line was gratitude keeps the garden.

Ask a child to draw an angel, and you'll usually get two wings. White, feathered, one on each side, like a bird's. It's the picture from a thousand paintings and greeting cards. Surah thirty-five opens with angels too, and in its very first verse it breaks that picture open. Not two wings. Two, or three, or four. And then a line that suggests the count doesn't stop there. The surah is called Fatir, the Originator, the One who splits creation open from nothing.

Verse one praises Allah, the Originator of the heavens and the earth. Then, Pickthall: "Who appointeth the angels messengers having wings two, three and four. He multiplieth in creation what He will." Notice the word messengers. In the Qur'an, angels aren't decoration. They carry things: revelation, mercy, sometimes warning. The Arabic says mathna, wa thulath, wa ruba', in twos, and threes, and fours. Then the open door: yazidu fil-khalqi ma yasha', He adds to creation whatever He wills. Many commentators read that as a hint that four isn't a limit. A hadith gives one example. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Mas'ud reports that the Prophet ﷺ saw Jibril in his true form with six hundred wings. The verse and the hadith aren't giving an anatomy lesson. Muslims believe angels are real but unseen, made of light, and that what anyone knows of them comes only from revelation. The point is humility about the pictures in your head: whatever you imagine, creation is larger, and still being added to. This week ran the same way. The mothers of the believers, Umm Salamah's question, a blessing that starts with Allah and the angels before it reaches anyone on earth. Mountains singing with Dawud. A termite that knew what the jinn didn't. A dam that broke when thanks ran dry. Again and again, the world in these surahs is bigger and stranger than the picture you walked in with.
screen: `HE ADDS TO CREATION AS HE WILLS.`

segments.voice: If you can, step to a window or outside and watch one bird fly: how the wings move, how often, how it turns. If no bird is near, picture the last one you saw. Then close your eyes with the line, He adds to creation as He wills, and let it widen whatever picture you're holding.
Mathna, the word for 'in twos,' opening Surah Fatir's list of the angels' wings: in twos, and threes, and fours. Today's word.
Your line: he adds to creation as he wills. Six hundred wings, in one report. That's the week.
